metas.name: Alaska - Alaska Gen 4
metas.note: Generation 4 coverage in Alaska is concentrated around the city of Anchorage. (As of April 25')
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Alaska - Alaska Shitcam
metas.note:
Shitcam is only found around Anchorage and Fairbanks, and parts of the road that connects them.

NOTE: This map shows all places where this camera can be found. Keep in mind coverage may be updated in some places, therefore you may come across regular coverage in places highlighted here.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Alaska - Anchorage Fire Hydrant
metas.note: Fire hydrants in Anchorage are typically pale pink or pale yellow in colour.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Alaska - Fairbanks Fire Hydrant
metas.note: Fire hydrants in Fairbanks are commonly either bright yellow or a combination of colours (most commonly yellow and blue).
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: California - San Diego Warning Sticker
metas.note: Almost all plates in San Diego County and southern Orange County have this warning plate, similar to those in Wisconsin. These are unique within California.
metas.footer: Credit: california: the greatest country in the united states by allie

metas.name: California - San Francisco Architecture
metas.note: Row Houses and other buildings in San Francisco are often in the style of Victorian architecture, with many bay windows, turrets, and ornate exterior details. These homes are built close together and can be very colourful.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: License Plate Meta
metas.note: The US, as well as most of the Americas, uses short licence plates, in contrast to longer European ones. Each US state has their own unique licence plate design. Some of these are recognizable through the blur, and are thus worth learning. Around half of the states also do not require front plates, which can also be useful in determining the state.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: Palms
metas.note: Palm trees are common in coastal areas of the Southeastern states, as well as the Desert Southwest region. Shown here is the Mexican Fan Palm, which is most common in California and along the Gulf Coast, but other palm tree types have a similar range.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Alabama Pole Plates
metas.note: You can see these fine plates with a round part on the side on most poles in Alabama and I have never seen anything like this elsewhere.
metas.footer: From: 28 SECRET US METAS by Ulork

metas.name: United States - Alabama Vertical End of Guardrail
metas.note: Guardrails in Alabama feature vertical yellow and black patterns, distinguishing them from other southern states. Note: This only applies within the Southern states
metas.footer: From 12 Infrastructure Metas for USA by Kratsooo

metas.name: United States - Alaska Northern Trees
metas.note: Trees in Alaska are generally thinner and have less broad leaves than those seen in the other 49 states.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Appalachian Fence
metas.note:
Dark-coloured wooden fences with several horizontal wooden supports are common in farming areas of central and southern Appalachia, stretching from Pennsylvania to Georgia.

NOTE: These types of fences can be found elsewhere to a lesser extent, so use other clues before guessing.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Appalachians
metas.note:
The Appalachian mountain range is a low mountain range that runs through the eastern states. The general landscape consists of low, forested mountains, with beech and oak trees being a common sight.

NOTE: Houses in the south generally have less storeys. New England architecture, commonly consisting of wood panelling, high roofs and a porch, is also more common toward the north, especially in New England.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - ATV Signs
metas.note: These green ATV Route signs are unique to Wisconsin.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Black Tar
metas.note: A black stripe can sometimes be seen in between the two yellow, middle road lines in California.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Brownstone Buildings
metas.note: Brownstone buildings are typically row houses or government buildings made out of various types of brick and sandstone. They are most commonly found in dense urban areas of the Northeast US, as well as Chicago.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - California Stripes
metas.note: Utility poles in California usually have markings at the bottom of the pole that consist of 3 yellow stripes.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Canola
metas.note: Along the Canadian border in North Dakota, and rarely Montana, fields filled with short yellow canola flowers (Brassica napus) can commonly be seen from the road.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Central Appalachians
metas.note: In the Appalachian area stretching from southern New York to southern Virginia, there are a lot of forest-covered rolling hills, with flat valleys dividing them. A majority of the ridges are oriented Southwest to Northeast.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Central Valley
metas.note:
Central Valley, California can be recognized by its Mediterranean climate. This is reflected in its agriculture, seen in the vineyards and olive trees that can commonly be found here.

In addition, rolling hills can be seen toward the edges of the valley.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Concrete Paving
metas.note:
Concrete paving on main highways is much more common in Iowa than in other states.

NOTE: Concrete paving on residential streets is commonly seen throughout the Midwest states and parts of the East Coast.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Corn
metas.note:
Corn fields can most commonly be found in these regions:-Iowa

-North of Iowa

-Nebraska without NW
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Cotton
metas.note: Cotton is a crop that produces large fields of fluffy white flowers. It is most commonly produced in coastal Southeast States, the Lower Mississippi River Valley, Western Texas, and parts of California and Arizona.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Diamond Bollard
metas.note:
The most common type of roadside bollard in South Dakota and Montana features a dark metal post with a white diamond on each side of the top.

NOTE: These bollards can be found to a lesser extent in other western states.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Dormant Grass
metas.note: Grass that is used in lawns in the southern US (colloquially known as Bermuda and St. Augustine grasses) go dormant in the winter months. This causes the lawns to turn beige or light brown in winter; whereas grasses used in more northern areas of the US stay much greener in winter.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Double Sign Posts
metas.note:
Signs attached to two signposts can be seen in Michigan. Not all signs are attached to two signposts.

NOTE: Double signposts can also be seen in other states, but are not as common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Douglas Fir
metas.note:
Extremely tall conifer trees (Douglas firs) with a dark brown bark, and dark green leaves, can most commonly be seen in Cascadia. Notably, they can also be found in northern California, Idaho and as far east as Montana.

Beware that they are also commonly found in British Columbia.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Golden Fields
metas.note:
Agricultural golden fields can commonly be seen in eastern Washington.

NOTE: Flat areas of northern and eastern Oregon can have a similar appearance.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Great Basin
metas.note: The Great Basin, centred around Nevada, can be recognized by the tall, sometimes snow-capped mountains in the background. There are dry, but grassy, and slightly shrubby plains leading up to the mountains.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Great Basin - Green
metas.note: Within the Great Basin, greener mountains can be seen in Idaho and central Utah.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Great Basin - Oregon
metas.note: Within the Great Basin, more gradual, rocky hills can be seen in Oregon.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Great Plains
metas.note: The Great Plains are in the middle of the United States and stretch from the Canadian border in the North, to central Texas in the South. This area is primarily flat with few trees. Some areas feature agriculture fields, while others feature dry and barren grassy fields.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Green Bollard
metas.note: Green bollards are common and (almost) unique to Idaho and Colorado, they exist in different forms, not only the one on this picture.
metas.footer: From: 28 SECRET US METAS by Ulork

metas.name: United States - Green/Red Rectangular Signs
metas.note:
Maine, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts use small green and red rectangular signs to mark the ends of bridges and guardrails.

NOTE: Not all bridges and guardrails in these states will have these markers.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - H-Reflector
metas.note: Snowplowable raised pavement markers can only be found on highways in the eastern states shown in the image. They are built into the road and somewhat resemble the letter H.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Hanging Lights
metas.note:
Many large intersections in Michigan have stop lights and signs that hang from wires that stretch across the middle of the intersection. These markers are commonly in yellow boxes.

NOTE: These are not completely unique to Michigan, but are most commonly seen there
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Hawaii Antenna
metas.note:
A stubby antenna can be seen in most Generation 3 coverage on Hawaii.

NOTE: The antenna is not always visible, so make sure to look out for other clues before guessing. (This antenna can also be seen in Cambodia, New Zealand, and US National Parks)
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Hawaii Smallcam
metas.note: Hawaii also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front, with parts of the black car being visible. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Hawaiian Place names
metas.note:
Hawaii is the only state to use its own language, though English is still predominantly used. Most place names are in Hawaiian, so you can spot it on street signs, and other road markers.

Hawaiian is a vowel-oriented language that only uses eight consonants: H, K, L, M, N, P, W, and (ʻ), called an ʻOkina.

Every Hawaiian word ends in one of 5 vowels: A, E, I, O, or U.

Each vowel can also have a macron over it: Ā, Ē, Ī, Ō, and Ū.

These vowels are often combined to make Diphthongs. I.e. UI, AI, AE, etc...
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Idaho Rectangular Bollard
metas.note: These bollards with a rectangle on top are common in Idaho and can only be seen there in western US. The rectangle can be white or yellow. Montana has a similar yellow version, but the reflector is much larger.
metas.footer: From 28 SECRET US METAS by Ulork

metas.name: United States - Iowa Sidepost
metas.note: The signpost on the side, as shown below, is unique to the state of Iowa in the Plains and Midwest. (only applies if you are in the Plains or Midwest)
metas.footer: From: 12 Infrastructure Metas for USA by Kratsooo

metas.name: United States - Kansas Signpost Reflectors
metas.note: These white reflectors on signposts are unique to Kansas. They are most commonly seen on ‘stop’ signs in rural areas.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Kentucky Thin Strips
metas.note: Kentucky commonly uses thin strips on the edge of the road, which is unique to the state. These strips are not to be confused with long thin strips that do not reach the edge of the road, which can also be used in Kentucky but also elsewhere.
metas.footer: From: US Rumble Strip Meta Doc by drazi

metas.name: United States - Large Center Line Gap
metas.note:
Yellow lines with a noticeably larger gap in between them are most common in Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Oregon. They can also be found to a lesser extent in Washington, Alabama, and Michigan.

NOTE: Wide middle lines can also rarely appear in other states, so consider other clues before guessing.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Massachusetts Pole Plates
metas.note: These rectangular plates, which can be white or yellow, can be seen on the side of poles in eastern Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Connecticut. These plates can very rarely be seen elsewhere.
metas.footer: From: 28 SECRET US METAS by Ulork

metas.name: United States - Minnesota Bridge Marker
metas.note: In Minnesota, these yellow signs with vertical, black triangles are placed before bridges at most major river crossings and at the beginnings and ends of guardrail sections on large highways. (I have seen these in other states but they are upsidown)
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Minnesota Signpost reflectors
metas.note: On most rural ‘stop’ signposts in Minnesota, a black-and-white marker is attached to the posts horizontally. The shape may vary slightly.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Mississippi River Valley
metas.note: The Lower Mississippi River Valley is a very flat and open landscape with red soil in areas of Tennessee, Arkansas, Mississippi, and Northeast Louisiana. Corn and other crops are common in this area.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Nebraska Sandhills
metas.note: The Nebraska Sandhills are a recognizable region of rolling hills covered with prairie grass in the central-north part of the state.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Nevada Bollard
metas.note: This bollard is found in Nevada. It consists of a reflector on a thin stick. The reflector is a vertical rectangle that consists of a white field surrounded by a black outline.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - New England Rock Walls
metas.note:
In rural areas of Connecticut, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire, short rock walls are commonly visible adjacent to the road.

NOTE: These rock walls can be found rarely in adjacent states.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - New England Shingled Walls
metas.note:
Houses in coastal New England often feature shingle walls, which are layered wood panels overlapping each other.

A similar style of panelling can also be seen, however, having a wider range than the one shown above.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - No Center Lines
metas.note:
Some small roads in California lack a middle yellow line; instead only feature solid white lines on each side of the road.

NOTE: This can rarely be seen in other states, notably Kentucky
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - North Carolina Signpost white Signs
metas.note: White signs attached to signposts can commonly be seen in North Carolina.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - North Carolina Street Signs
metas.note:
North Carolina commonly uses a style of street signs showing street numbers and arrows in addition to the street name.

NOTE: Other states occasionally feature street signs with similar designs, so use other clues before guessing.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Number/Direction Street Signs
metas.note:
Streets in Utah and Idaho, particularly in urban areas, are often named by using a combination of a number and cardinal direction (i.e. ‘600 South.’)

NOTE: This style of street naming can be found rarely in other Western states.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Ohio Gap
metas.note: In Ohio, you can often see gaps in road lines where there is a RPM (raised pavement marker). It can also sometimes be seen elsewhere (Tennessee or New Jersey) but it is much rarer.
metas.footer: From: 28 SECRET US METAS by Ulork

metas.name: United States - Oil Pumpjack
metas.note: Oil pumpjacks are short, industrial-looking metal structures located at the surface of oil fields and are used to pump crude oil from the earth below. They are most common in western states, particularly in Texas, Eastern New Mexico, and North Dakota.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Oklahoma Fence
metas.note: Red metallic fences are very common in Oklahoma and the surrounding states, particularly Kansas, Texas, and Arkansas. This is not 100% so look for other clues before sending.
metas.footer: From 28 SECRET US METAS by Ulork

metas.name: United States - Oklahoma No Guardrail Reflectors
metas.note: Oklahoma has no guardrails with reflectors inside it. If you see a guardrail with reflectors, don’t guess Oklahoma.
metas.footer: From 12 Infrastructure Metas for USA by Kratsooo

metas.name: United States - Oklahoma Stop Sign
metas.note: In Oklahoma, you can often find a green rectangular sign with 3 rows of numbers attached to the back of stop signs at rural intersections
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Oregon Bollard
metas.note: This bollard is extremely common in Oregon and is almost exclusive to this state. It can rarely be seen in California (but usually when it is the case, it is not exactly this bollard, the white rectangle will be bigger or it won’t be all the way on top for example).
metas.footer: From 28 SECRET US METAS by Ulork

metas.name: United States - Oregon Roadlines
metas.note: These short and fine lines can often be seen in between Oregon roadlines which are usually wide, you can see similar lines elsewhere but it is useful to distinguish Oregon from surrounding states especially Washington who also often uses wide roadlines.
metas.footer: From 28 SECRET US METAS by Ulork

metas.name: United States - Oregon Speed
metas.note: Speed signs in Oregon often simply have the word ‘Speed’ instead of the standard ‘Speed Limit’.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Ouachita Mountains
metas.note: The Ouachita Mountains stretch from Eastern Oklahoma into West-Central Arkansas. Unlike the nearby Ozark Mountains, these mountains are typically more steep in nature and easier to see from a distance.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - PA Bollards
metas.note: Pennsylvania bollards are very common on guardrails and sometimes elsewhere. They can be white or yellow and are recognizable by their shape and black cap.
metas.footer: From: 12 Infrastructure Metas for USA by Kratsooo

metas.name: United States - PA Rectangular white signs
metas.note: Rectangular white signs can sometimes be seen attached to signposts at intersections in Pennsylvania. On top, the number of the converging state route is written.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Pacific Rainforest
metas.note:
Temperate rainforests are found in coastal areas of Washington, Oregon, and Northern California. These rainforests feature many broadleaf trees, large conifers, and ferns.

NOTE: These rainforests stretch north into coastal British Columbia and Southeast Alaska as well.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Prairie Pothole
metas.note: The area spanning from the Montana Border with Saskatchewan to the Western Great Lakes features many ‘prairie potholes.’ These are areas of low-lying wetlands that feature marshy grasses and small, shallow ponds.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Publix
metas.note: ‘Publix’ is a regional supermarket chain that has locations primarily in Florida and adjacent areas of the Deep South.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Pueblo Architecture
metas.note:
Pueblo Revival style houses are commonly seen in New Mexico. They are typically constructed of adobe or brick and concrete. They have rounded edges and flat roofs, and are usually sand-brown in colour.

NOTE: Pueblo style houses can also be seen in Arizona and Colorado to a lesser extent.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Rectangular Reflector
metas.note: These rectangular raised pavement markers are found in the south and west of the US and also in Massachusetts.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Reddish Soil
metas.note: Many parts of the Deep South, stretching from Oklahoma to South Carolina, have reddish soil. The exact tint of the soil can range from yellow to deep red.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Rice
metas.note: Rice production only occurs in a few areas of the US, so it is very useful for region guessing. It is typically grown in large, flat fields that resemble low prairies. It is only grown in north-central California and the Lower Mississippi River Valley in Arkansas, Louisiana, Texas, and Mississippi.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Rio Grande Valley
metas.note: The Rio Grande Valley in South Texas is extremely flat and features shrubby trees and agricultural fields. This area borders the Mexican state of Tamaulipas.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Rocky Mountains
metas.note: The area stretching from the Canadian border to Northern New Mexico is home to the Rocky Mountains. These jagged, rocky formations often feature many pine trees and visible snow all-year round at the highest peaks. Some areas of the Rocky Mountain Range are noticeably dry, with few trees.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Sagebrush
metas.note: Great Basin Sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata) is a short, shrubby blue-green bush that is common in the interior western United States.It is most common in arid areas.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Saguaro
metas.note: Saguaro cacti are most commonly shaped like tall, straight tubes with several branches extending from the main tube. They are most commonly found in southern Arizona, on the Sonoran border.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - SC Black Street Signs
metas.note: Black street signs with white text can commonly be found at intersections in South Carolina.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - SC Reflectors (No Roadlines)
metas.note: If you see a small road without roadlines that has Southern Reflectors in the middle, you will most likely be in South Carolina. In other states the reflectors will always be next to roadlines. Sometimes these roadlines can be faded so be careful.
metas.footer: 28 SECRET US METAS by Ulork

metas.name: United States - Shoprite
metas.note: ‘Shoprite’ is a regional supermarket chain that has locations in 6 states in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic region of the US; Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, and Maryland.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Short Stilts
metas.note: Similar in style to aforementioned stilt houses, houses with much shorter stilts are common in the western and central Gulf Coast. These houses typically feature short stilts made of concrete or wood (1-3 feet off the ground) and are primarily found in areas near the coast and any adjacent rivers.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Shotgun Houses
metas.note: Very narrow, one-storey houses made out of wood are called ‘shotgun houses.’ They are most common in and around New Orleans (LA,) Houston (TX,) Louisville (KY,) and the state of Mississippi.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Sloped Roofs
metas.note: Buildings with very large, sloped roofs are most common in the states of Oklahoma, Texas, and Louisiana. They can also be seen in neighbouring states to a lesser extent.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Southern Pines
metas.note: The loblolly pine (Pinus taeda), and longleaf pine (Pinus palustris), commonly referred to as southern pines in the community, are found throughout the southeastern US. They are a great way to recognize this region, as they are abundant, recognizable and mostly limited to this part of the country. They tend to be tall, with fluffy-looking clusters of pine needles.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Soy
metas.note: Soybeans are short, dark green crops organised in long rows and are found in similar regions where corn is grown. They are most common in the Eastern Plains, Midwest, Lower Mississippi Valley, and areas of the Mid Atlantic.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Spanish Colonial Revival
metas.note: Spanish Colonial Revival Architecture can be categorised as buildings with lightly-coloured stucco walls and red clay-tile roofs. They can be found in the desert southwest states of California, Nevada, Arizona, and Texas. You can also find similar types of buildings in Florida and coastal Georgia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Spanish Moss
metas.note: Spanish moss, appearing as greyish white drapes, can sometimes be seen on trees in the deep south.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Square Guardrails
metas.note:
Square guardrails are the most dominant (but not the only) type of guardrail in the states of New York and Wyoming. They have a long bar across the top, with several square legs supporting them.

NOTE: These guardrails can be found, to a lesser extent, in some adjacent states.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Stacked Triplexes
metas.note:
Older three story wooden houses, also called ‘stacked triplexes,’ are very common in urban areas of the Northeast. They are most prevalent in New York, Connecticut, Rhode Island, and Massachusetts.

NOTE: These types of houses are also somewhat common in cities in Atlantic Canada.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Stilt Houses
metas.note: Stilt houses can sometimes be seen on the coast. These are especially common toward the south, and on the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Tablelands
metas.note: The Southwest, centred around the Four Corners region of Utah, Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado, feature many mesas and tablelands. Often, these rock formations will be red in colour. Additionally, red soil is common in these areas.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Texas Bands
metas.note:
Yellow or red bands can commonly be seen around signposts in Texas.

NOTE: Similar reflectors can sometimes be seen in other states, such as Hawaii.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Texas Bumps
metas.note: These littles rectangular bumps on center lines are unique to Texas. You can see some round bumps in some other states but rectangular ones are only in Texas.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Texas Guardrail Bollards
metas.note: White Bollard + Grey/Yellow Square. These bollards are unique to Texas on guardrails in the southern United States.
metas.footer: From 12 Infrastrucuture metas for USA by Kratsooo

metas.name: United States - Texas Hills
metas.note: Just west of the metropolitan areas of Austin and San Antonio Texas lies a large area of dry, rocky hills featuring many yucca and prickly pear plants. Texas Live Oak trees are the predominant tree type in this area.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - Texas Pavement
metas.note:
Texan roads often have a grainy, ‘salt and pepper’-like road surface.

NOTE: Similar pavement can sometimes be seen in adjacent states such as New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Colorado.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Thick Center Lines
metas.note:
Some roads in West Virginia, Virginia, and Maryland use middle yellow lines that are thicker than traditional yellow road lines.

NOTE: These are not present on all roads in these states, and can be found elsewhere, so use this tip in conjunction with other clues.

metas.name: United States - Utah Bollard
metas.note: This bollard is unique to Utah.
metas.footer: From: 28 SECRET US METAS by Ulork

metas.name: United States - Utah Idaho Bollard
metas.note: This type of bollard with a white square on top is unique to Utah and Idaho. If the square is not totally on top then it should be Idaho.
metas.footer: From 28 SECRET US METAS by Ulork

metas.name: United States - Vermont Small Green Stop Signs
metas.note:
Vermont features small rectangular green signs on stop sign posts with three rows of horizontal numbers. The top row of numbers correlates to the highway or road number that the road with the stop sign intersects with. For example, this image is taken from Vermont State Road 116, looking towards the intersecting road.

The State of New York uses similar style signs. However, these signs can be attached to different types of sign posts (town entry signs, highway signs, etc.)
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Vertical House Numbers
metas.note:
Properties in rural and exurban Ohio, Lower Michigan, and Indiana commonly feature a vertically-oriented metal sign with white numbers, indicating the house number of the adjacent building. These signs are most commonly blue or green, and are commonly attached to mailboxes.

NOTE: These may be rarely found in other states.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Virginia Rectangle white signs
metas.note: Rectangular white signs can sometimes be seen at intersections in Virginia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Washington Bollard
metas.note: The state of Washington uses bollards that consist of a white or brown post with a white rectangle on the front of the bollard, and two smaller white or silver squares on the back of the bollard.
metas.footer: Source: PlonkIt

metas.name: United States - WI Bollard
metas.note: These simple white bollards with black reflectors are unique to Wisconsin.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - WI Property Markers
metas.note:
A horizontal blue, red, or green sign can commonly be seen at the ends of driveways in Wisconsin and the Michigan peninsula. The house number is present, in addition to either the town name and or the road name (usually.)

NOTE: Nearby states often use similar markers, but typically lack any town or street name information and only feature numbers.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - WI Warning Pole Plate
metas.note: A rectangular white metal plate, with an orange rectangle and diamond, can be seen on most poles in Wisconsin and the Michigan peninsula.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - WI/MO Letters
metas.note: Wisconsin and Missouri are the only two states that use a lettering system (A - ZZZ) for their county highways. Wisconsin signs typically have the word ‘county’ above the letter, while Missouri signs typically do not. The borders of the signs also vary slightly.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Wyoming Bollard
metas.note: Roadside bollards in Wyoming often feature a dark metal pole with a white circular reflector at the top. The top of the metal pole is sometimes painted white or grey, which is unique to Wyoming.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - Yellow Posts
metas.note: Yellow posts like this one are common in Colorado and can be seen more rarely in Utah or Texas. It can rarely be seen in other states. (Very rare and not the most consistant; I have also seen it twice in Virginia)
metas.footer: From: 28 SECRET US METAS by Ulork
